opening.headline: Distinguishes between the scope within the platform where AI app quality and cost can be viewed, and the scope outside that platform.
body: When operating an AI app, you'll often receive a flurry of questions about yesterday's slow responses, this month's token costs, and declining answer quality. The first step should be to verify what insights your existing data platform currently provides before introducing a new monitoring tool.

In this course, we will examine Snowflake AI Observability, Databricks MLflow traces, Unity Catalog storage, evaluation runs, and data profiling, and establish guidelines that define the scope of built-in observability and external tool integration.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain Snowflake AI Observability and Databricks tracing storage methods
It is possible to distinguish between built-in observation within the platform and the application scope of external tools.

screens.title: How to assess the quality and cost of AI apps within the platform
screens.lead: After launching the AI app, we examine the first question that the team receives. Read the paragraphs sequentially and verify up to the final reference box.

visual.alt: This is a diagram showing three questions about actively operating AI apps directed towards two data platforms.
labels: How much did it cost this month?

paragraphs: Once an AI app is deployed into the operating environment, the team soon accumulates three key questions: What happened yesterday with requests that were slow or anomalous? What was the token cost this month? Did the response quality degrade? These are questions that only become relevant after the app has been developed.

At this point, many teams immediately want to add new observability tools. However, it's more appropriate to first verify what their existing data platform is already showing. The platform's built-in observability features answer a significant portion of the questions.

Snowflake includes AI Observability features within its Cortex functionality. Conversation traces can be viewed in Snowsight, dataset-level evaluation can be performed, and credits and tokens can be queried in the Account Usage view. Databricks uses MLflow Tracing as the foundational layer for observability, storing traces in Unity Catalog tables and managing them via SQL and authorization systems.

This course aims to distinguish where built-in monitoring of two platforms covers and where external tools are required. Finally, it confirms that the monitoring data itself is an asset that requires access control.

callout.label: Note
callout.text: In this class, the term "observation" includes recording at the request unit level (trace), evaluation at the dataset level, tracking of data changes over time, and usage aggregation.

screens.title: What is the difference between built-in observation tools and external observation tools?
screens.lead: First, think about it yourself. You don't need to enter an answer. When you select a question, the instructor's thoughts are presented.

items.prompt: Thought experiment 1: Where will observation data be stored?
items.answer: Built-in observability stores data within the platform where it is already written. In Snowflake, agent traces are accumulated in the SNOWFLAKE.LOCAL.AI_OBSERVABILITY_EVENTS account, and in Databricks, traces can be stored in a Delta table within Unity Catalog. External tools typically copy data to separate services for storage. Differences in storage locations lead to variations in retention periods, costs, and compliance requirements.

items.prompt: Thought Exercise 2: Who can access that data?
items.answer: Built-in observation follows the platform's role and authorization hierarchy. Traces stored in Unity Catalog are accessed based on schema and table permissions. External tools must manage their own accounts and authorization models separately, therefore, data containing prompts and responses must be verified in two places regarding who can read it.

items.prompt: Thought experiment 3: Can we see apps running outside the platform?
items.answer: Built-in observability fits best with apps that use the platform's features. Snowflake documents that not all Cortex observability capabilities are supported on the same observability surface. However, custom-built apps can send telemetry to the platform account via traces in TruLens or OpenTelemetry formats, so it does not necessarily mean that built-in observability must be abandoned simply because an app runs outside the platform.

screens.outro: Based on the three axes, let's now verify what the two platforms are actually displaying.

screens.title: What Snowflake AI Observability shows
screens.lead: When reading the table from top to bottom, note that the observable aspects for each Cortex feature vary.

data.notes: AI observability is a set of capabilities that answers questions such as what happened in operational requests, how well the model performs on test data, what the cost per request is, and whether guardrails blocked the request. Custom AI applications you build can send telemetry to TruLens whether they are hosted inside Snowflake or outside Snowflake, and in this case, traces and evaluation results are stored in the AI_OBSERVABILITY_EVENTS table. When aggregating costs, you must base your calculations on usage views rather than the events table. Trace delivery follows best-effort practices, which means the sum of events in the events table may be less than actual usage.

screens.outro: Now let's see how the same question is addressed in Databricks.

screens.title: Databricks Tracing and Unity Catalog Storage
screens.lead: Toggle to compare traces saved to an MLflow experiment versus those saved to Unity Catalog.

visual.alt: An agent's execution is recorded as a span tree and flows into one of two storage locations.

states.label: Save to Experiment
states.body: This is the method for storing traces in MLflow experiments. There is a limit of 100,000 traces per experiment. Traces can be queried via the MLflow UI and Python SDK. Access control is performed at the experiment level. Additionally, OpenTelemetry compatibility is noted as not supported in the documentation. While this approach is sufficient for lightly checking traces during development, the limit becomes a burden for long-term retention and analysis in operational workloads.

states.label: Saved to Unity Catalog
states.body: This method stores traces in Unity Catalog's Delta table in OpenTelemetry format, and Databricks recommends it for both new and operational workloads. There is no storage limit, and traces can be analyzed using SQL, Genie Code, AI/BI dashboards, and Spark-based tools, in addition to MLflow UI and SDK. Access control is managed through schema and table permissions. Experiments still serve as entry points, but the data itself is governed as a table—meaning traces are also stored as a single table.

screens.outro: Now that I understand how traces accumulate, I will move beyond request-level observations to observations based on batches and time units.

screens.title: Evaluation execution and data profiling
screens.lead: Select an item to expand and read about the two observation methods that differ from request-unit observations.

items.title: Quality assessment execution: batch job that evaluates quality using a dataset
items.body: Evaluation execution is a batch job that runs the app once for each input in the dataset, and then the scorer evaluates the results to fill in the outcomes. In Snowflake, you can view results in the Evaluations tab of Cortex Agents, and in MLflow, through the evaluation UI. An evaluation dataset consists of a list of items containing inputs and expectations, and unlike tracing, it measures quality using predefined test data rather than actual operational requests.

items.title: Data profiling: Observations over time to see changes
items.body: Databricks data profiling calculates summary statistics for tables over time windows and displays changes over time. It enables tracking of null ratios, value distributions, and drifts relative to benchmarks. A baseline table can be specified separately, and in inference profiling, the data used for training or validation can serve as an appropriate baseline.

items.title: Profile type: Time series, inference, snapshot
items.body: Time series profiling divides a table with a timestamp column into time windows for computation. Inference profiling targets a model's request log table, where each row represents one request and includes input, prediction, and optionally a ground truth label. Snapshot profiling processes the entire table whenever any table is updated, with a maximum table size of 4TB. Larger tables must use time series profiling.

items.title: What changes: request-level versus trend-level
items.body: Tracing provides detailed insight into the internal flow of a single request and is used to identify the root cause of individual failures. Profiling shows how model inputs and predictions evolve over time and how data quality degrades gradually. The metrics tables generated by profiling capture these changes, trigger alerts, and assist in narrowing down the root cause. The two approaches are not alternatives but complementary.

screens.outro: Since we've verified the functionality, let's now jointly work through an example of determining whether built-in monitoring is sufficient.

screens.title: When built-in observation is sufficient versus when external tools are required
screens.lead: The instructor explains three cases in sequence. Click the following arrow to advance to the next case and follow the reasoning basis.

steps.title: First, establish judgment criteria.
steps.body: We ask three questions in sequence. First, does the app run within the platform? Second, does it actually provide the observed functionality that users need? Third, do we need to view apps from multiple platforms on a single screen? If the first two questions are answered affirmatively, then built-in observability is a candidate. If the third question is also affirmative, then we consider external tools.

steps.title: Example A: Team using only Cortex Agents
steps.body: This team's agents are deployed via the Agent API or CoWork, and conversation threads, turns, and execution spans are automatically logged into AI_OBSERVABILITY_EVENTS. Operational conversations can be debugged in the Observability tab, dataset evaluations can be run in the Evaluations tab, and usage can be checked in CORTEX_AGENT_USAGE_HISTORY. Since all requirements are resolved within the platform, built-in observability is sufficient.

steps.title: Example B: Databricks Agent and Unity Catalog Storage Traces
steps.body: The agent runs in Databricks and logs traces to a Unity Catalog table. The team aggregates latency and token usage into a SQL data warehouse, builds an AI/BI dashboard, and connects alerts—all within the same platform. With built-in capabilities for querying, visualization, and alerting, separate observability tools are not required.

steps.title: Case C: A team with agents dispersed across multiple platforms and their own servers
steps.body: Some agents operate on Snowflake, some on Databricks, and the rest on on-premises servers. Each platform's built-in observability only provides insights within its own domain, making it difficult to compare across the entire stack on a single screen. In this case, we review a design that collects traces in a common OpenTelemetry format and aggregates them using external observability tools. This approach complements existing built-in observability rather than disabling it.

steps.title: Explanation summary: First verify the scope.
steps.body: Whether built-in observations are sufficient is not a question of tool superiority, but rather a matter of scope. It can be judged based on three aspects: the app's location, the observation capabilities provided by its features, and the necessity of an integrated view. When making judgments, refer to usage reports such as Account Usage, and also keep in mind the distinction between tracing and its roles in debugging and quality analysis.

screens.outro: Finally, let us examine whether the observed data itself is accessible to anyone.

screens.title: Observation data is also subject to the platform's governance.
screens.lead: Selecting the two passages emphasized in the following explanation demonstrates how each passage affects the outcome.

data.text: Traces contain the user's prompts and model responses verbatim. When stored in Unity Catalog, users with schema and table permissions can view all traces in that table, regardless of the experiment. Access to Snowflake's AI_OBSERVABILITY_EVENTS and Account Usage views is also governed by the account's roles and permissions. Choosing where to store observability data is therefore part of access-control design.

marks.note: This means trace control is managed at the table level, not at the experiment level. If traces from different experiments are collected into the same table, users with only table permissions can read traces from all experiments. It is safer to isolate sensitive team traces into separate schemas.

Whether Snowflake can read observation data is determined by the role permissions granted on event tables or the Account Usage view. Since no separate observation tools are required, existing role designs are directly applied, making the assignment of roles to observation personnel a design consideration.

marks.span: the user's prompts and model responses verbatim
marks.note: Traces are both logs and data assets containing user inputs. Since personal information or sensitive data may be mixed into prompts, their storage location, access permissions, and retention period must be managed at the same level as other business data.

screens.outro: Now I will summarize everything discussed so far.

screens.title: Key points and reflection
screens.lead: Let's quickly review the core content of the lecture once more to conclude.

paragraphs: Snowflake's observability varies by feature. Cortex Agents use the Observability and Evaluations tabs in Snowsight, while built-in AI functions and REST APIs show usage in Account Usage. Therefore, viewing both the dashboards and usage metrics together provides a complete picture.

Databricks recommends recording each step of an agent using MLflow Tracing, and storing the traces in a Unity Catalog table for operational workloads. This enables analysis via SQL and access control through permissions.

Evaluation execution is a batch job that assesses data quality against a dataset, while data profiling tracks changes in data over time. It provides traceability at the request level and answers different questions.
Finally, remember that observation data contains prompts and responses and is therefore subject to access control.

Therefore, when reviewing new observation tools, we first check three things before looking at the feature list: on which platform our app runs, whether that platform already provides the necessary observation capabilities, and who has access to the data. Following this order helps reduce unnecessary tool introductions and ensures external tools are added only where truly needed.

callout.label: Judgment criteria
callout.text: Whether the app is running within the platform, whether it provides a required observation surface, or whether an integrated view is needed. These three criteria distinguish the scope of built-in observability from external tools.

checks.q: In an app that directly calls Cortex AI Functions via a REST API, will conversation span-level traces appear in Snowsight's Observability tab?
options: It appears. All Cortex calls are recorded as spans in the same event table.
It doesn't show up. Only credit, token, model, and request ID remain in Account Usage.
It appears. However, it is displayed only after the evaluation execution has been run once.
It doesn't show up. This call leaves no usage records.
checks.explain: Automatic thread and span recording is a feature of built-in observability targets such as Cortex Agents, while AI Functions or REST API calls only leave usage-level information in the Account Usage view.

wrong.0: Span records correspond to built-in features similar to agents and do not apply to all calls.
wrong.2: The evaluation execution status and trace recording are separate.
wrong.3: Trace is absent but usage remains in Account Usage.

checks.intro: Please take a look at the table showing the feature-based observation differences between Snowflake's components. The results are not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes. The remaining record varies depending on the calling method.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Sorry, please recall that agent tracing and usage logging are stored in different locations.

checks.q: Pair up the terms and explanations related to Databricks tracing.
right: Delta tables have no limits and can be analyzed using SQL and dashboards, managed through schema and table permissions.
A foundational data layer that records inputs, outputs, delays, tokens, and costs at each stage of an agent
Each experiment has a trace limit of 100,000 and access control is at the experiment unit level.
checks.explain: MLflow Tracing is the recording itself, and you can choose to store it in either the experiment store or Unity Catalog store. For operational workloads, the latter is recommended.
checks.intro: Explore the terminology and storage methods of Databricks traces. Results are not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes, you correctly distinguished between the record itself and its storage location.
checks.incorrectFeedback: There is a mismatch. Please compare the logging functionality with the characteristics of the two storage locations again.

checks.q: When traces are stored in Unity Catalog, which user can view all traces of a given table?
options: Only the owner of this MLflow experiment
All users logged into the workspace
Only the developer of the traced application
Users with schema-table permissions are able to access all experiments regardless of experimentation.
checks.explain: In UC Storage, access is defined by schema and table permissions rather than by experimental units. Since traces include both prompts and responses, selecting the storage location is equivalent to designing access control.

wrong.0: Experimental unit access control is a characteristic of experimental storage schemes.
wrong.1: You cannot see it if you don't have the permission.
wrong.2: It's not about the writer's status; it's about table privileges.

checks.intro: Consider the scope of access to Unity Catalog storage traces. Results are not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes. Access is not experimental; it is determined by table privileges.
checks.incorrectFeedback: This option is either a characteristic of the experiment storage format or a description unrelated to permissions. Please verify the unit of permissions again.

glossary.def: A set of features that enables you to view request tracing, batch evaluation, usage, and guardrails activity within Snowflake Cortex.
This approach stores MLflow traces in OpenTelemetry format within Delta tables and manages them using SQL, schema, and table permissions.
A batch job that runs the app on each input of the dataset and collects the scorer's results.
A Databricks feature that calculates summary statistics for tables on a per-time-window basis to track distribution changes and drift.
Record of individual execution steps that constitute a trace, containing start and end timestamps as well as input and output information.

misconceptions.myth: With built-in observation, all Cortex features can be viewed on the same screen.
misconceptions.fact: Each function has a different observation surface. Cortex Agents show traces in Snowsight, but built-in AI Functions and REST API only record usage in Account Usage.

misconceptions.myth: Tracing is a tool used only for debugging during development.
misconceptions.fact: Databricks documentation states that debugging, evaluation, and operational monitoring are all built upon evidence captured in traces.

misconceptions.myth: The trace table is merely a log storage and has no relation to governance.
misconceptions.fact: Traces saved in Unity Catalog are data assets with schema and table permissions, and require access control due to the presence of prompts and responses.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: Built-in observability in the platform enables tracing, monitoring, and usage to be verified within the platform itself.
Databricks tracing is stored in Unity Catalog tables and can be queried and managed using SQL and permissions.
If you need apps outside the built-in scope or an integrated view across multiple platforms, consider external tools.
Observation data is also data governed by the platform.
